sections.title: What are BFS and DFS?
sections.content:
BFS and DFS are the two fundamental ways to explore a graph. Every graph algorithm — topological sort, shortest paths, cycle detection, connected components — is built on one of these two strategies.

**DFS (Depth-First Search)** dives deep: follow one path as far as it goes, backtrack on a dead end or visited node, try the next branch. Naturally recursive (call stack mirrors recursion) or iterative with an explicit stack. Right tool for: cycle detection, path existence, connected components, topological sort, backtracking.

**BFS (Breadth-First Search)** explores wide: visit all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. Uses a queue. Because it explores level by level, it naturally finds the **shortest path** in an unweighted graph. Right tool for: shortest path unweighted, nearest nodes, flood fill, multi-source problems.

Both are O(V+E) — visit each vertex once, traverse each edge once. The difference is exploration order, which determines what problems each solves optimally.

Almost all interview problems use an **adjacency list** — `graph[node]` gives a list of neighbors. O(V+E) space. An adjacency matrix is O(V²) and rarely needed in interviews.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use BFS for shortest path in an unweighted graph or level-by-level exploration. Use DFS for path existence, cycle detection, connected components, or exhaustive exploration. For grids, DFS is simpler to code recursively; BFS is better when minimum steps is asked.

sections.title: Graph Representation and Traversal Mechanics
sections.content:
## Adjacency List

Build from edge list `[[u,v],...]` as first step:
```
graph[u].push(v); if (!directed) graph[v].push(u);
```
Space O(V+E). Iterating neighbors of a node: O(degree).

## DFS — Critical Rule

Mark node as visited **before** recursing/pushing. Marking after allows cyclic graphs to recurse infinitely.

**Post-order**: process node after all descendants are done — essential for topological sort.

## BFS — Critical Rule

Mark neighbors as visited **when enqueuing**, not when dequeuing. Waiting until dequeue allows the same node to be enqueued multiple times.

Shortest path: `dist[neighbor] = dist[current] + 1` when enqueuing. First time BFS reaches a node is the shortest path.

## Connected Components

A single BFS/DFS explores one component. To find all: iterate over all nodes, start a new traversal for each unvisited node, count traversal starts.

## Cycle Detection — Undirected

During DFS, if a visited node is encountered that is not the current node's parent, a cycle exists. Track parent to avoid the trivial A→B→A false positive.

## Cycle Detection — Directed

Node coloring: **white** (unvisited), **gray** (in current DFS path), **black** (fully processed). Encountering a gray node means a back edge exists — cycle detected.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: DFS with explicit stack and BFS with index-based queue (avoids O(n) shift). Both mark visited before enqueue/push. buildGraph creates adjacency list from edge list.

items.name: Multi-Source BFS
items.description: Enqueue all source nodes at distance 0 instead of a single source. BFS expands from all sources simultaneously — used for 'nearest land cell from water', 'walls and gates', 'rotting oranges'.

items.name: Bidirectional BFS
items.description: Run BFS from both source and destination simultaneously, alternating layers. Stop when frontiers meet. Reduces explored nodes from O(b^d) to O(2 × b^(d/2)) — significant speedup for large sparse graphs.

items.name: DFS with Color States
items.description: Assign each node 0 (white/unvisited), 1 (gray/in path), 2 (black/done). Encountering a gray node during DFS signals a back edge and a cycle in a directed graph.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: Both visit each vertex once (O(V)) and traverse each edge once (O(E)). BFS queue holds at most O(V) nodes. DFS stack is O(V) in worst case (a path graph). In grid problems V = rows × cols and E = 4V (4-directional), so O(V+E) = O(V).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Not marking nodes visited before enqueuing/pushing — in cyclic graphs this causes infinite loops; in DAGs it causes exponential blowup as the same node is processed multiple times.
BFS: marking visited on dequeue instead of enqueue — the same node can be enqueued multiple times before processing, giving wrong shortest-path distances.
Undirected cycle detection: treating the parent edge as a cycle — B sees A is visited but A is B's parent. Track parent and skip it.
Directed vs undirected cycle detection require different approaches — simple visited boolean works for undirected; directed graphs need gray/black coloring.
Not resetting visited array between separate traversals in a loop — reuse causes components to appear already-visited.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Topological sort is a direct application of DFS post-order on a directed graph. You already know cycle detection and the DFS skeleton; topological sort adds post-order stack logic and Kahn's BFS-based alternative.
